title: Equations of horizontal and vertical lines

beats.say: Open like a teacher: two lines whose equations are shockingly short. Curious, friendly. No questions.

lines.say: Today we meet two lines with really short equations. One says x equals two, and the other says y equals minus three. They look too simple to be lines at all. But they are, and understanding them clears up a lot of confusion about gradients later.

beats.say: Plot-and-spot: the points (2,-1), (2,0), (2,3) share the same x. Mark the 2s IN PLACE, then name the line x = 2. The picture shows the points. No questions.

lines.say: Look at these three points. Before I say anything, look at their coordinates, and see what they have in common.
The x-coordinate is the same every time. It's a two. The y-coordinates are all different, but x never changes.
So if you stand on any point of this line, your x-coordinate is two. Every single point.
That's why this line is named x equals two. Its equation just tells you what x always is. It's a vertical line, standing straight up and down.

lines.text: x = a  is a VERTICAL line
lines.say: In general, x equals any number a is a vertical line. The equation names the one x-value every point shares.

beats.say: Now the flat one. Points (-2,-3), (0,-3), (4,-3). Mark the -3s in place, name y = -3. Mirror the vertical beat. No questions.

lines.say: Now a different set of points. Negative two, minus three. Zero, minus three. Four, minus three. What stays the same this time?
This time it's the y-coordinate that never changes: always minus three. The x-coordinates wander about, minus two, zero, four.
So every point on this line has y equal to minus three.
The line is named y equals minus three. It runs flat across the page, parallel to the x-axis, like a calm horizon.

lines.text: y = c  is a HORIZONTAL line
lines.say: In general, y equals a number c is a horizontal line.

beats.say: Gradient of each. Vertical: from (2,-1) to (2,3): rise 4, run 0, 4 / 0 is undefined. Horizontal: from (-2,-3) to (4,-3): rise 0, run 6, gradient 0. Use the first picture step to show the vertical line while working. No questions.

lines.say: Let's find the gradient of the vertical line. Rise over run. Take two points on it, (2, −1) and (2, 3).
The rise is how far we go up: from minus one up to three, that's four.
The run is how far we go across. Both x-values are two, so we go nowhere sideways: zero.
So the gradient is four divided by zero, and nobody can divide by zero. We say the gradient is undefined.
Now the horizontal line. Take (−2, −3) and (4, −3).
The rise is zero, because we stay at the same height.
The run is six, from minus two across to four.
Zero divided by six is just zero. A flat line has gradient zero.

beats.say: A friend says a vertical line has gradient 0 because it 'doesn't slope'. Test it on (2,1) and (2,5). The picture steps through. Detective tone, no questions.

lines.say: A friend of mine says: a vertical line has gradient zero, because zero means no slope. Let's test it. Take (2, 1) and (2, 5).
The rise is four. The run is zero.
If four divided by zero did equal zero, then by checking, zero times zero would have to equal four. Which is nonsense!

lines.text: No number × 0 gives 4, so 4 ÷ 0 is undefined
lines.say: No number multiplied by zero ever gives four. So the division simply has no answer.

lines.text: Flat line: gradient 0.   Vertical line: undefined.
lines.say: Zero gradient is for flat lines. A vertical line isn't flat, it's the steepest line there is, and its gradient is undefined.

beats.say: Summary of the three facts, plus why a vertical line is not the graph of a function. Reuse x = 2 with its three points. No questions.

lines.text: y = c:  horizontal,  gradient 0,  parallel to the x-axis
lines.say: One. y equals c: a horizontal line, gradient zero, parallel to the x-axis.

lines.text: x = a:  vertical,  gradient undefined,  parallel to the y-axis
lines.say: Two. x equals a: a vertical line, gradient undefined, parallel to the y-axis.

lines.text: x = 2  pairs with y = −1, 0, 3, ... infinitely many
lines.say: Three. A vertical line like x equals two matches the single x-value two with infinitely many y-values: minus one, zero, three, and on and on.

lines.text: One x must give ONE y for a function  →  x = 2 is not a function
lines.say: A function must give just one y for each x. The vertical line breaks that, so it's a line, but it isn't the graph of a function.

beats.say: Do one TOGETHER, the line through (-5, 8) and (-5, -3). The picture shows the points. Questions are written on the board first.

lines.say: Now you help me. A straight line goes through (−5, 8) and (−5, −3).
Yes, the x-coordinate is minus five in both.

ask.prompt: What do the two points have in common?
ask.onMiss: Ask: look at the first number in each pair.

lines.say: So the equation names that x-value.

ask.prompt: What is the equation of the line through them?
ask.onMiss: Ask: the line is named after what every point shares.

lines.say: Same x, so no run at all.

ask.lookFor: Undefined: the run is 0, and you cannot divide by 0.
ask.onMiss: Ask: what is the run between points with the same x?

lines.text: It is parallel to the y-axis
lines.say: A vertical line is parallel to the y-axis.

ask.prompt: Which axis is it parallel to?
ask.onMiss: Ask: is the line vertical or horizontal?

beats.say: The child works alone: line through (1, 6) and (7, 6): equation, gradient, which axis; then the equation of the x-axis. Hints only if stuck.

lines.say: Your turn to lead. A line goes through (1, 6) and (7, 6).
Both points have the same height, six.

ask.prompt: What is the equation of the line?
ask.onMiss: Ask: which coordinate is the same in both points?

lines.say: The rise is zero.

ask.onMiss: Ask: what is the rise? What is the run?

lines.text: It is parallel to the x-axis
lines.say: And a horizontal line runs parallel to the x-axis.

ask.prompt: Is it parallel to the x-axis or the y-axis?
ask.onMiss: Ask: is y = 6 a flat line or a standing-up line?

beats.say: Explain the two why-questions in the child's own words. Reward reasoning.

board.text: Say it in your own words

lines.text: flat line: gradient 0.  vertical line: undefined
lines.say: Last two, the 'why' questions.

ask.prompt: Why is the gradient of a flat line 0, but a vertical line's gradient undefined?
ask.lookFor: Flat line: rise is 0, and 0 ÷ run = 0. Vertical line: run is 0, and dividing by 0 is impossible.
ask.onMiss: Ask: what are the rise and the run for each kind of line?

lines.text: x = 2 gives many y values, so it is not a function
lines.say: And one more.

ask.prompt: Why is the vertical line x = 2 not the graph of a linear function?
ask.lookFor: One x-value (2) goes with infinitely many y-values, but a function gives exactly one y for each x.
ask.onMiss: Ask: how many y-values sit above x = 2 on that line?
